def: The assumptions about the data that an architecture or learning method builds in, such as locality in a convolution or order in a recurrent network; strong bias learns from less data but caps flexibility.
The number of layers a signal passes through in sequence; more depth allows more steps of composition but adds latency and makes training harder.
The size of each layer's hidden vector (the model dimension d in a transformer); parameters grow with the square of width.
The ratio of width to depth; published frontier decoders sit around 100 to 130 hidden units per layer, and loss depends only weakly on it at fixed size.
A skip path that adds a layer's input to its output, h + F(h), giving gradients a direct route back and letting a layer default to the identity (He et al. 2015).
In a transformer, the running vector per token that every attention and MLP block reads from and adds its output back into.
Gradients shrinking geometrically as they flow back through many layers or time steps, because each step multiplies them by a factor below one; early layers stop learning.
Gradients growing geometrically through many layers or time steps because each step multiplies them by a factor above one; causes loss spikes and divergence.
Deeper plain networks reaching higher training error than shallower ones, an optimisation failure rather than overfitting, which residual connections fixed.
Normalising each feature using the mean and variance over the current batch (Ioffe and Szegedy 2015); central to CNNs, awkward for language models.
Normalising each example's feature vector by its own mean and variance (Ba et al. 2016), so behaviour is identical in training and inference and for any batch size.
A cheaper layer-normalisation variant that rescales by the root mean square of the features without subtracting the mean; used in Llama-family models.
Placing normalisation at the input of each residual branch, leaving the residual stream untouched; more stable at depth than the original post-norm transformer.
An experiment that changes one component while holding everything else fixed, to measure that component's effect; at a frontier lab, run compute-matched at several scales.
Automatically proposing and evaluating architectures with search or reinforcement learning; effective at small scale, rare at frontier scale because each candidate must be trained.
A way of scaling initialisation and per-layer learning rates with width so the best hyperparameters stay roughly constant, allowing tuning on a small proxy (Yang et al. 2022).
Rosenblatt's 1958 single-layer classifier: a weighted sum of inputs compared with a threshold, trained by nudging weights after mistakes.
Computing the gradient of the loss for every weight by applying the chain rule backwards through the network; popularised by Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams (1986).
A network built from convolution layers that apply one small shared filter at every position of a grid; the standard design for images before vision transformers.
Sliding one small kernel of weights across an input and taking a weighted sum at every position; encodes locality, weight sharing, and translation equivariance.
The region of the input that can influence one output unit; it grows with each stacked convolution or pooling layer.
A network that reads a sequence one step at a time, updating a hidden state with the same weights at every step.
Long short-term memory (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber 1997): an RNN with gates and an additively updated cell state so information and gradients survive many steps.
A layer that computes, for each position, a softmax-weighted average of other positions' values, with weights from how well a query matches each key (Bahdanau et al. 2014).
An architecture of stacked self-attention and MLP blocks with residual connections and normalisation, processing all positions in parallel (Vaswani et al. 2017).
A sequence layer built on a linear recurrence ht = A ht−1 + B xt; trains in parallel and runs at constant memory per token. Mamba (Gu and Dao 2023) makes the parameters input-dependent.
A network for graph-structured data in which each node repeatedly updates its representation from messages sent by the nodes it is linked to.
The GNN layer of Kipf and Welling (2017): a degree-normalised average over each node's neighbours and itself, followed by a shared weight matrix.
The general GNN template (Gilmer et al. 2017): compute messages along edges, aggregate them at each node with a permutation-invariant function, then update the node.
Node representations in a deep GNN converging to nearly the same value because every layer averages over neighbours, erasing the differences between nodes.
Information from a node's exponentially growing k-hop neighbourhood being compressed through a few edges into fixed-size vectors, which limits long-range reasoning in GNNs.
A GNN that weights each neighbour's message with learned attention scores instead of fixed averages (Veličković et al. 2018).
A GNN that samples a fixed number of neighbours and learns aggregation functions, so it scales to huge graphs and to nodes unseen in training (Hamilton et al. 2017).
